title: The Idol That Comes Alive: Radha, Denishawn, and an East Assembled from Photographs
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Pin Oaks Farm and the Delsarte Inheritance

stops.name: Newark, New Jersey: born to a woman doctor and a machinist
stops.date_confidence: The day and month are firm; the year is not. Wikipedia and the modern biographical consensus give 1879, older reference works give 1877 or 1880, and Encyclopedia.com gives 'probably 1878'. Wikipedia places the birth in Newark and the upbringing at Pin Oaks Farm; a research note in the pool had conflated the two and put the birth on the farm, and that conflation is corrected here.
stops.campa: She is born Ruth Dennis on a January morning in Newark, to Ruth Emma Hull Dennis, a physician trained when very few women were, and Thomas Laban Dennis, a machinist and inventor. The parents are not married. The child is carried out to a small farm called Pin Oaks in the country near Somerville, and it is the farm and not the city that raises her. Reference books will later give her birth year as 1877, as 1878, as 1880. She never corrects them with any consistency, and no document in reach settles it.
suggested_refs: The Ruth St. Denis Papers, 1880-1968, UCLA Library Special Collections

stops.name: Pin Oaks Farm, near Somerville: the mother's physical culture
stops.date_confidence: The date orders the childhood and is not an event date. The farm and the household's reform-minded, physical-culture character come from the dossier's synthesis of Suzanne Shelton's biography and St. Denis's own memoir; neither was reachable directly in this pass, and the exact parcel of Pin Oaks Farm was not pinpointed. The coordinates are the Somerville locale, not a surveyed site.
stops.campa: The farm is bohemian and reform-minded, run by a mother who has studied medicine and physical culture and who puts her daughter in nothing that constricts. The girl works at the Delsarte exercises her mother sets her, relaxation and succession and the poses that are supposed to correspond to states of the soul. She invents melodramas with herself in every part and performs them where there is nobody to watch. It is what a child does on a farm with no neighbours and a mother who believes the body means something. Nobody in the house calls it training.
suggested_refs: Genevieve Stebbins, Delsarte System of Expression (1885), the manual by which the system reached American households
sources: Suzanne Shelton, Divine Dancer: A Biography of Ruth St. Denis (1981), via dossier
Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (1939)

stops.name: New York: Genevieve Stebbins dances The Dance of Day
stops.date_confidence: The year is attested; the venue and the month are not established by any source reached, and the coordinates are the Midtown pin the atlas already carries for the transmission of the Delsarte system into America, not a located theatre.
stops.campa: Genevieve Stebbins, who had the Sorbonne manuscript from Delsarte's widow and published the Delsarte System of Expression seven years earlier, dances The Dance of Day before a New York audience. In it is a girl of thirteen up from a New Jersey farm. What the girl sees is a woman alone on a stage, without partner, without plot, moving in a vocabulary built out of a Frenchman's theory of the soul. She calls it afterwards the real birth of her art life.
suggested_refs: Genevieve Stebbins, Delsarte System of Expression (1885)
sources: delsarte.journey.json, 'The world after: Stebbins, Laban, Muybridge and the notated body'

stops.name: Worth's Family Theatre and Museum, New York: the skirt dance
stops.date_confidence: The 1894 professional debut at Worth's is attested verbatim by Wikipedia; the month is not. The coordinates are a flagged problem: the figure carried in the research pool, 40.7215 / -73.9975, is in Greenwich Village and is wrong for a Sixth Avenue dime museum in the Tenderloin. No source stating the street address was reachable this pass, HathiTrust returning 403 on the trade directory, so the pin here is the Sixth Avenue and West 30th Street vicinity and should be read as approximate.
stops.campa: At fifteen she goes on the professional stage. For the next ten years she works the circuit upward, dime museum to vaudeville to touring melodrama to Broadway, learning the trade from the bottom of it. At Worth's the work is a skirt dance among the waxworks and the freak exhibits and the short turns: yards of fabric raised and swirled under limelight, four or five minutes, then off for the next act. That is what the variety houses want in 1894, and it is what she can do.
suggested_refs: Worth's Family Theatre and Museum, Sixth Avenue, New York, in the 1890s dime-museum trade

stops.name: David Belasco's company: Zaza, and Madame Du Barry
stops.date_confidence: The Belasco engagement is attested; its start year is approximate, the period running from the late 1890s to about 1904 or 1905. The coordinates are the Broadway theatre district and not a located house: Zaza (1899) and Madame Du Barry (1901) both predate Belasco's own West 44th Street theatre, which opened in 1907 as the Stuyvesant, so the venues for these two productions are not fixed here.
stops.campa: David Belasco takes her into his company and she plays in Zaza and in Madame Du Barry, on Broadway and on the road. Belasco is the American theatre's great manufacturer of atmosphere: coloured light, slow fades, real incense, a stage built so that an audience believes it has walked into somewhere. He is also a master of publicity, and he understands that a performer is a thing to be framed. She stays with him into the middle of the next decade, learning the lighting and learning the framing, and she is still playing supporting parts when she goes.
suggested_refs: David Belasco's productions of Zaza (1899) and Madame Du Barry (1901)
sources: Suzanne Shelton, Divine Dancer (1981), via dossier

stops.name: Buffalo, New York: Egyptian Deities behind the soda fountain
stops.date_confidence: The touring context and the existence of the Egyptian Deities advertising image are documented; the moment itself rests entirely on St. Denis's own repeated retelling, in lectures and in her 1939 memoir, with no contemporaneous record of the drugstore, the date, or the poster she saw. The month is unknown and the address of the drugstore is unknown; the pin is the centre of Buffalo.
stops.campa: The company is touring Madame Du Barry and she goes into a Buffalo drugstore for a soda. On the wall above the fountain hangs an advertisement for Egyptian Deities cigarettes: a goddess on a throne, framed by a sort of pylon, drawn by a commercial artist who has never seen Egypt either. What she takes off the wall is not Egypt. It is the discovery that a divinity can be posed, framed, lit and sold. She sits with the glass in front of her and does not drink it.
stops.quote: It must have contained a potent magic for me. I stopped with my soda half consumed and stared and stared.
stops.quote_source: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (Harrap, 1939), ch. IV
suggested_refs: The Egyptian Deities cigarette advertisement, showing an enthroned Isis under a pylon
sources: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (1939), ch. IV, archive.org dli.ministry.22233

stops.name: New York: she takes the name, and builds a Hindu goddess instead
stops.date_confidence: The adoption of the stage name and the turn to solo work are placed at 1905 by the standard chronology and are tagged reconstruction rather than attested: no document fixes the month, and the shift from supporting player to soloist was gradual. That Egypta was conceived first and shelved for cost, with Radha made in its place, is her own account. The coordinates are a Midtown placeholder.
stops.campa: She drops out of the supporting roles and takes a new name, St. Denis, saint and stage billing in one word. The Egyptian spectacle she has planned, Egypta, costs more than anyone will give her, so she makes a Hindu one instead, out of museum bronzes, photographs, and Delsarte. Radha is a temple idol who comes alive for the length of a dance, moves through the five senses one by one, renounces them, and goes back to being stone. She has never been to India. She has read about it and looked hard at pictures of it.
stops.quote: I conceived of her as an idol in her temple, who for a brief time was infused with life and danced a message for her devotees.
stops.quote_source: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (Harrap, 1939), ch. IV
suggested_refs: Egypta, the unbuilt Egyptian spectacle of 1904-1905, shelved for cost and staged only in 1910
sources: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (1939), ch. IV

stops.name: Hudson Theatre, West 44th Street: Radha, The Incense, The Cobras
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction left open. The exact date of 22 March 1906 and the Hudson Theatre venue come from Christena Schlundt's performance chronology as relayed by the dossier; Wikipedia's own article says only that Radha was 'performed in 1906' and places her Hudson Theatre appearance in 1909. Radha also had earlier vaudeville showings in early 1906, so 'premiere' overstates what this matinee was. The coordinates are the Hudson Theatre at 139-141 West 44th Street per Wikipedia, replacing a Herald Square figure carried in the pool that was about a kilometre off.
stops.campa: At the Hudson Theatre she gives Radha with The Incense and The Cobras, barefoot, to music lifted from Delibes's Lakme. There are bells, garlands, a bowl of incense, a jewelled bodice, and rings worn as snake heads on her fingers. The piece has already been shown in vaudeville earlier in the year; this is the matinee that gets written about. Society women come and critics come, and within weeks she is a name. She has no company, no ballet training, and no licence from any tradition she is representing.
stops.quote: She was the human soul, forever seeking union with the divine, which was Krishna.
stops.quote_source: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (Harrap, 1939), ch. IV, on Radha
suggested_refs: Christena L. Schlundt, The Professional Appearances of Ruth St. Denis and Ted Shawn: A Chronology (1962)
Jane Desmond, 'Dancing Out the Difference: Cultural Imperialism and Ruth St. Denis's Radha of 1906', Signs 17:1 (1991)

stops.name: London: the divine dancer, and the German houses
stops.date_confidence: The European tour and its strong London and German-speaking reception are attested; no specific venue, and no month, was independently confirmed this pass, and the coordinates are a West End placeholder. The tour is usually given as running 1906 to 1909. Paris is not named in any source reached for St. Denis herself, and no Paris stop is entered here despite the city's central place in the careers of the other American solo dancers of the decade.
stops.campa: She sails for Europe and finds there what New York had given her only in part. London receives her as the divine dancer. The German-speaking houses receive her harder still, Berlin and the cities around it filling for three years running. Continental critics have a category ready before she arrives, the sacred dancer out of the East, and they file her under it without checking anything. She is twenty-seven, working entirely alone, and the fees are large enough to keep her abroad until 1909.
stops.quote: I feel when I dance before great audiences that I am delivering a wordless message of immortality; that life is harmonious without end; that my body is indeed the willing servant of the mind.
stops.quote_source: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (Harrap, 1939), p. 241 approx.
suggested_refs: The German-language press notices of St. Denis's 1906-1909 tour, the making of the 'heilige Tanzerin' reputation
sources: Suzanne Shelton, Divine Dancer (1981), via dossier

stops.name: London: watching Isadora Duncan in a nearly empty house
stops.date_confidence: St. Denis's account of seeing Isadora Duncan in London, while she herself was engaged at the Scala and Maud Allan was filling the Palace, is her own, written down thirty years later in An Unfinished Life, ch. VII, pp. 117-118. The year within the 1906-1909 tour is not fixed by any source reached and 1908 orders the segment only. The pool's citation of ch. XI for these passages was wrong and is corrected to ch. VII here.
stops.campa: In London she goes to see Isadora Duncan, who is dancing to a sparse house at the small Duke of York's while Maud Allan plays to packed ones at the Palace. St. Denis is at the Scala, well paid and well noticed. Mary Fanton Roberts will later set the pair as Dionysiac and Apollonian, Isadora the first and Ruth the second, and St. Denis copies the judgment into her own book thirty years afterwards. She sits in the thin audience and watches, and writes that Duncan evoked in that pitifully small room visions of the morning of the world.
stops.quote: In one arm's movement was all the grace of the world, in one backward flinging of her head was all nobility!
stops.quote_source: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (Harrap, 1939), ch. VII 'I Belong to America', p. 118
suggested_refs: The Duke of York's Theatre, London, where Duncan played to a sparse house during St. Denis's Scala engagement
sources: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (1939), ch. VII, pp. 117-118, archive.org dli.ministry.22233

stops.name: Hudson Theatre, New York: a Salome of her own, in the Salomania year
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia attests the 1909 Hudson Theatre Salome performance and the wider Salome craze; the month and the run length are not established by any source reached.
stops.campa: Salomania is on. Every variety house in Europe and America has a woman with seven veils, in the wake of Wilde and Strauss and the courts that banned them both. St. Denis, three years back from Europe and needing New York work, gives her own Salome at the Hudson, in the house where Radha was seen. She is meeting the market, and meeting it in her own idiom, the temple rather than the harem. Whether anyone out front could tell the one idiom from the other, the surviving notices do not say.
suggested_refs: The 1908-1909 Salome vogue in Anglo-American variety and concert dance

stops.name: Denver: Ted Shawn in the house
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia's article states directly that in 1911 a young dancer named Ted Shawn was impressed by seeing St. Denis perform in Denver. The month, the venue, and the programme are not established. The pool's geography lens had tagged this reconstruction while its chronology lens tagged it attested; the two disagreed and the attested reading is taken here.
stops.campa: A young man called Ted Shawn, thirteen years her junior, sits in a Denver house and watches her work. He had been studying for the Methodist ministry and came to dance late, by way of an illness that took the use of his legs and exercises that gave them back. He decides that night what he wants. It will take him three years to reach her. Nothing in the encounter is mutual, and nothing about it is recorded on her side: she dances, collects the fee, and goes on to the next city on the route.
suggested_refs: Ted Shawn's own account of the Denver viewing, in his writings on Denishawn
sources: Suzanne Shelton, Divine Dancer (1981), via dossier

stops.name: Mason Opera House, Los Angeles: a seventeen-year-old in the audience
stops.date_confidence: The year is attested through Martha Graham's own account; the month and day of the performance are not established by any source reached. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from martha_graham.journey.json, which carries the Mason Opera House at 127 South Broadway.
stops.campa: On South Broadway she dances an East assembled out of postcards, temple photographs, brass and incense. In the house sits Martha Graham, seventeen years old, at the first dance performance of any kind she has ever attended, in defiance of a father who holds that the theatre is not respectable. Graham decides that evening on a life in dance. She will not begin training for another five years, and when she does it will be at this dancer's own school. St. Denis knows nothing of it.
suggested_refs: The Mason Opera House, 127 South Broadway, Los Angeles
sources: martha_graham.journey.json, 'Mason Opera House, Los Angeles: Ruth St. Denis on the stage'

stops.name: New York: Ted Shawn arrives with a letter and an intention
stops.date_confidence: The 1914 New York meeting is attested by Wikipedia's Ted Shawn article; the month is not, and March here only places the meeting before the 13 April first concert. Coordinates are the Manhattan theatre district, not a located address.
stops.campa: Ted Shawn comes to New York to find her. He is a dancer of modest reputation who has toured ballroom exhibition work up and down the western circuits; she is the most famous solo dancer in America, and she needs a partner, a manager, and a man strong enough to lift. He becomes all three. She takes him first as a student, and pupil before partner is the order that everything between them keeps for fifty years. The first joint concert is a month or two off. The marriage is five months off.
suggested_refs: Ted Shawn's account of his first approach to St. Denis, 1914

stops.name: United States: the first joint concert
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The date of 13 April 1914 comes from the dossier's use of Shelton and Schlundt; the venue and city are not confirmed by any source reached, and the coordinates are a Manhattan theatre-district placeholder rather than a located house.
stops.campa: They dance together in public for the first time. She is thirty-five and has worked alone for a decade; the duet is a form she does not entirely trust and has spent ten years not needing. For that decade her career has been one woman on a stage and an audience that came to see exactly that. What the pairing hands her is a company, a school, a touring apparatus, and a name that can be split down the middle and sold twice. They will be married in four months. The concert comes first.
suggested_refs: Christena L. Schlundt, The Professional Appearances of Ruth St. Denis and Ted Shawn: A Chronology (1962)

stops.name: New York: the marriage that runs fifty-four years
stops.date_confidence: The date and the New York location are attested by Wikipedia's Ted Shawn article; the ceremony site was not located, and the coordinates are a general New York City pin.
stops.campa: They marry in August, four months after the first joint concert, and go straight back on the road. Neither will ever divorce the other, though within twenty years they will separate domestically and artistically and live largely apart, he in the Berkshires with a company of men, she in Los Angeles with her choirs of women. The arrangement is also a partnership contract for a business neither of them has founded yet. There are no children. The marriage runs fifty-four years, to her death.
suggested_refs: Edwin Myers Shawn, married to Ruth St. Denis 13 August 1914, never divorced

stops.name: Portland, Oregon: the two names fuse on a bill
stops.date_confidence: The date and the Portland origin of the compound name come from Encyclopedia.com's Denishawn history page. Note that the school founded that summer in Los Angeles was not yet called Denishawn, so at this point the word is a billing and a company label only. Coordinates are the centre of Portland; no venue is named in the source.
stops.campa: On tour in Portland their two names are joined on a bill and the compound holds: Denishawn. It begins as a convenience of billing for a ballroom act, a printer's economy, half of hers and half of his. Within a year it will be a school; within twelve, an institution that a generation of dancers define themselves by walking out of. The word is made in Oregon on a February night, in the ordinary business of selling tickets. Nobody present writes down whose idea it was.
suggested_refs: The Portland playbill of 6 February 1915, on which the Denishawn compound first appears

stops.name: 600 St. Paul Avenue, Los Angeles: the school opens under her own name
stops.date_confidence: Attested for summer 1915 and for the address; the month is not fixed. Wikipedia's Denishawn article is explicit that the institution founded here was the Ruth St. Denis School of Dancing and Its Related Arts, not the Denishawn School, and the pool carried that name wrongly. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from martha_graham.journey.json. Flagged: an OSM geocode of 600 St. Paul Avenue returns 34.0534 / -118.2608, some 500 metres east of the inherited pin, and the discrepancy is left unresolved in favour of atlas consistency.
stops.campa: In an old Spanish house on St. Paul Avenue, west of downtown Los Angeles, they open a school. Its name at the founding is the Ruth St. Denis School of Dancing and Its Related Arts; the shorter word arrives later. The curriculum is everything at once, ballet barre and Delsarte and Dalcroze eurhythmics, yoga, Spanish, Egyptian, Japanese, whatever the two of them have seen and can teach. There is a platform in the open air, and the students work on it in the California morning before the heat comes up.
suggested_refs: The Denishawn house at 600 St. Paul Avenue, in the old Crown Hill district of Los Angeles

stops.name: The Palace Theatre, New York: the Egyptian Ballet and the Pyrrhic Dance
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The 1916 Egyptian Ballet, containing Tillers of the Soil and Shawn's all-male Pyrrhic Dance, and a Denishawn engagement at New York's Palace Theater are both reported for 1916, but no source reached confirms that the ballet premiered at the Palace or in which city it opened; the pool's own geography lens left the premiere city as Los Angeles or New York. The month is unknown. Coordinates are the Palace Theatre on Broadway at 47th Street.
stops.campa: The Egyptian spectacle reaches a stage at last, twelve years after the cigarette poster and in a form she can afford. In it she and Shawn dance Tillers of the Soil, two peasants working a Nile field in flat profile, arms and heads turned as they are turned in tomb painting. Shawn also sets a Pyrrhic Dance for men only, the first appearance of the male company he will eventually build for himself and take away. Denishawn is playing vaudeville's first house, two shows a day.
stops.quote: This seated image of Isis, a superficial, commercial drawing for a cigarette company, opened up to me in that moment the whole story that was Egypt.
stops.quote_source: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (Harrap, 1939), ch. IV
suggested_refs: Tillers of the Soil, the St. Denis and Shawn duet from the Egyptian Ballet (1916)

stops.name: 600 St. Paul Avenue: Martha Graham enters the school
stops.date_confidence: Graham's arrival in the school's second summer, 1916, is attested; the month within that year is not. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from martha_graham.journey.json. The 'over six years' figure for her time in the company is Encyclopedia.com's.
stops.campa: Martha Graham comes to the school five years after seeing her at the Mason Opera House. She is twenty-two, late for a beginner, and by every account graceless at first. St. Denis takes little interest; it is Shawn who sees what is in her and gives her parts. Graham stays more than six years, pupil and then instructor, and takes in the whole eclectic apparatus so completely that she will need the next decade to cut it out of herself. At her own first concert she will say that everything she did was influenced by Denishawn.
suggested_refs: Martha Graham's own account of her Denishawn years, in Blood Memory (1991)

stops.name: West Lake Park, Los Angeles: the second house, and the picture business
stops.date_confidence: The second Los Angeles school near West Lake Park, with a garden, tennis court and outdoor dance platform, is attested by Wikipedia's Denishawn article, which dates it only to the 1910s; 1918 orders the segment and is not an attested year. Coordinates corrected to the centre of West Lake Park, now MacArthur Park, replacing a figure in the pool that sat 1.3 kilometres north. Louise Brooks's seasons with the touring company, 1922-23 and 1923-24, are from Encyclopedia.com.
stops.campa: The school outgrows the first house and takes a second near West Lake Park, an old place with a garden, a tennis court, and a dance platform in the open. Los Angeles in these years is filling with people who intend to be looked at, and Denishawn sits exactly where the temple meets the studio lot. Louise Brooks will pass through the touring company as a teenager on her way to the pictures and to Berlin. Most of the actual teaching happens outdoors, on the platform, in the mornings.
suggested_refs: The second Denishawn house at West Lake Park, Los Angeles

segments.name: Ishtar, and the Gates of the East

stops.name: United States: Ishtar of the Seven Gates
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The work and the year are reported by Wikipedia and the dossier; the premiere city, venue and month are not established by any source reached, and the coordinates are a Manhattan theatre-district placeholder.
stops.campa: She stages Ishtar, the Babylonian goddess who goes down through seven gates into the underworld, and at each gate the doorkeeper takes something from her. It is the most severe thing she has made, a spectacle whose whole subject is the removal of spectacle. She is forty-four. The school is prospering and the marriage is starting to come apart. On stage, in front of a paying house, she surrenders crown, necklace, girdle, rings and robe, and comes through the seventh with nothing on her.
stops.quote: My final use to art is impersonal, for when I dance I am really an abstraction, a creature set apart from time and space, unrelated to human things in the ordinary sense.
stops.quote_source: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (Harrap, 1939), p. 241 approx.
suggested_refs: Ishtar of the Seven Gates (1923), the descent through the gates
sources: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (1939)

stops.name: Bombay: the company lands in India
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the reader should treat the whole Asian sequence with the same caution. India is attested as one of the tour countries by Encyclopedia.com, but Bombay as a stop is inferred as the principal port of entry. The date orders the segment only: neither the month, nor this stop's position in the itinerary, is established by any source reached, because Christena Schlundt's chronology and Jane Sherman's Soaring, which carry the city-by-city dates, could not be obtained this pass.
stops.campa: The company lands in India. It is the first time she has set foot in the country. For nineteen years she has been dancing Radha, a Hindu temple idol built out of photographs and a Frenchman's theory of gesture, before audiences who took it for the thing itself. The Denishawn programme goes up in the theatres of a colonial city, and Radha is on it, unaltered. Now the country is around her: the heat, the port, the crowds, and living traditions of dance she has no training in and cannot read.
suggested_refs: Jane Sherman, Soaring: The Diary and Letters of a Denishawn Dancer in the Far East, 1925-1926 (Wesleyan, 1976)
Christena L. Schlundt, chronology of Denishawn appearances

stops.name: Colombo, Ceylon: the diary that outlasts the tour
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Ceylon is attested among the tour countries; Colombo is inferred as the principal port and is not confirmed. The date orders the segment only, as with the whole Asian sequence. Jane Sherman's published diary is attested as a 1976 Wesleyan University Press title but was not read directly this pass.
stops.campa: In Ceylon the company plays to the audience a colonial port assembles: British officials, Burgher families, Ceylonese in the expensive seats. The dancers are young, most of them under twenty-five, and several of them keep diaries. One of those dancers, Jane Sherman, will publish hers half a century later, and it is out of her pages rather than out of St. Denis's own accounts that the itinerary can be reconstructed at all. St. Denis writes very little down while it is happening.
suggested_refs: Jane Sherman, Soaring: The Diary and Letters of a Denishawn Dancer in the Far East, 1925-1926 (Wesleyan, 1976)

stops.name: Rangoon, Burma: where the devotion is not theatre
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Burma is attested among the tour countries; Rangoon is inferred as the principal city and is not confirmed. The date orders the segment only. Nothing in the sources reached records St. Denis's own reaction to any particular Burmese site, and the campa says so rather than inventing one.
stops.campa: Burma. The company plays Rangoon, and the gold of the Shwedagon stands over the whole city, visible from the river and from the streets and from the stage door. She has been performing Asian devotion as theatre since 1906, and she is now in a place where devotion is not theatre at all, where people are doing on an ordinary Tuesday morning what she has spent two decades staging under coloured light for money. What she made of that, nothing in the surviving record says.
suggested_refs: The Shwedagon Pagoda, Rangoon, standing over the city the company played in 1925-1926

stops.name: Singapore: the steamer circuit, and authentic dances of the Orient
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Malaya is attested among the tour countries; Singapore is inferred as the principal city. A correction is flagged in the naming: in 1925-1926 Singapore belonged to the Straits Settlements, a separate Crown colony, and was not part of Malaya, so the pool's label 'Singapore, Malaya' is a geographical error and is not repeated here. The date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: Singapore, capital of the Straits Settlements and not of Malaya, whatever the tour lists say. The company is on the British steamer circuit now, moving port to port with a stage manager, trunks of costume, and a repertory that has to be reset for whatever house they find at the other end. The advance billing sells authentic dances of the Orient. Denishawn is the first American concert dance company several of these cities have seen. Java, China, Japan and the Philippines are still ahead of them.
suggested_refs: Denishawn advance publicity for the 1925-1926 Asian tour

stops.name: Batavia, Java: court dance that will not yield
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Java is attested among the tour countries; Batavia is inferred as the principal city. The date orders the segment only. That the company encountered Javanese court dance is a reasonable inference from the itinerary and is not documented in any source reached; what the encounter did or did not do to St. Denis's own practice is stated here as an open question rather than as a finding.
stops.campa: Java, under the Dutch. Here the company meets a court tradition so disciplined and so slow that the Denishawn vocabulary has nothing at all to answer it with: gamelan, the shifting weight, gesture measured in fractions of a beat across hours. She is forty-six and has built a career on the proposition that the East can be read off its images. In Java the images have their originals standing beside them. The company sits and watches, and the gamelan goes on for hours.
suggested_refs: Javanese court dance at the kraton, encountered by touring Western companies in the 1920s

stops.name: Shanghai: the attitude of Kuan Yin
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. China is attested among the tour countries and photographs of St. Denis in the Kuan Yin persona are reported for this period by the dossier; Shanghai is inferred as a principal touring city and is not confirmed. The date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: China is the sixth country on the tour. Photographs survive from this leg showing her in the attitude of Kuan Yin, the bodhisattva of compassion, and she will go on dancing Kuan Yin for the rest of her life. The figure is not invented here. It is confirmed here, which is a different operation altogether, and the one she has been running since the Buffalo drugstore. In the pictures she is seated, one knee raised, the hand shaped into a mudra copied off statuary.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Ruth St. Denis as Kuan Yin, from the 1925-1926 tour, NYPL Dance Division
sources: Dossier, on the Kuan Yin and Kwannon personae

stops.name: Tokyo: the same goddess in another language
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Japan is attested among the tour countries; Tokyo is inferred as a principal city and is not confirmed. The date orders the segment only. That the Kwannon persona was developed on the Japanese leg is the dossier's reading, not a documented sequence.
stops.campa: Japan. The Kwannon of the Japanese temples is the same bodhisattva under another name, and she adds the persona beside the Chinese one, a goddess held in two languages at once. The houses are large. Japan in 1926 has its own appetite for Western concert forms and its own centuries of stage dance, and the traffic runs in both directions in ways nobody on the American side of the footlights is equipped to see. She is dancing six nights a week and the tour is most of a year old.
suggested_refs: Kwannon, the Japanese form of Avalokitesvara, source of St. Denis's late goddess persona

stops.name: Manila: the tour closes
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Philippines are attested among the tour countries; Manila is inferred as the principal city, and its placement last in the sequence follows Encyclopedia.com's order of listing rather than an attested itinerary. The date orders the segment only. Encyclopedia.com's claim that Denishawn was the first American company to present Western concert dance in several of these countries was not independently checked.
stops.campa: The Philippines close the Asian leg, an American colony at the end of a circuit of British and Dutch ones. In under two years the company has crossed India, Ceylon, Burma, Malaya, Java, China, Japan and the American colony in the Pacific, playing colonial theatres, garrison halls and opera houses, and it sails home the most travelled dance company in the United States. It is the last thing the two of them build together. The dancers who kept the diaries will be running companies of their own inside a decade.
suggested_refs: Jane Sherman, Soaring (Wesleyan, 1976), the tour seen from inside the company

stops.name: Stevenson Place, the Bronx: Denishawn House
stops.date_confidence: The 1927 Bronx school on Stevenson Place is attested by Encyclopedia.com and by Wikipedia's Denishawn article; no street number or coordinates for Stevenson Place could be pinned this pass, and the pin here is a general Bronx placeholder. The month is unknown. That Humphrey and Weidman ran much of the building's teaching is attested; the financing detail is the dossier's framing.
stops.campa: They put up Denishawn House on Stevenson Place, at the northern end of the city, a purpose-built plant for a school that has outgrown improvising. It costs more than they have, and the money comes out of the touring and out of borrowing. The touring that pays for it takes them away from each other and away from the teaching, and it is Doris Humphrey and Charles Weidman who run much of what actually happens in the rooms. The building opens in 1927. The market goes in 1929.
suggested_refs: Denishawn House, Stevenson Place, the Bronx, opened 1927

stops.name: New York: the pupils walk out
stops.date_confidence: Graham's 1923 departure and the 1928 Humphrey and Weidman break are both attested; the exact months are not established by any source reached, and 1928 here stands for the sequence of departures rather than a single day. The coordinates are the Denishawn House pin, which is where the losses were felt, not where any of the departing dancers went. Jose Limon's enrolment year at the Humphrey-Weidman school is not attested in the atlas file that carries it.
stops.campa: Martha Graham had gone in 1923, to the Greenwich Village Follies and then to a studio of her own. In 1928 Doris Humphrey and Charles Weidman go too, taking with them a technique built on fall and recovery that owes nothing whatever to temple attitudes. From Humphrey's own school the line runs on to Jose Limon, who never met St. Denis and inherits her regardless. By 1928 the dancers who will define American modern dance for the next thirty years have all left the building.
suggested_refs: Doris Humphrey and Charles Weidman, the 1928 break from Denishawn

stops.name: United States: Denishawn stops existing
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction left open. Sources give the end of Denishawn variously as 1930, 1931 and 1932, because the school, the company and the marriage did not dissolve in a single act, and the dossier flags the discrepancy explicitly. The coordinates repeat the Denishawn House pin for want of a place where the dissolution can be said to have happened.
stops.campa: It ends without an act to mark it. The school closes, the company stops touring, Shawn goes off to a farm in the Berkshires, and the marriage that had also been a business becomes neither one. The Depression takes the money. The dancers she trained have gone. She is fifty-two and without an institution for the first time in sixteen years. Sources put the collapse at 1930, at 1931, at 1932, because school and company and marriage did not come apart together.
stops.quote: In the beginning of my career, had I waited for praise I should never have been born. Had I rested upon the praise that I received I should never have advanced.
stops.quote_source: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (Harrap, 1939), ch. XIV 'Denishawn House', p. 330
suggested_refs: The dispersal of the Denishawn holdings, 1930-1932

stops.name: United States: the Society of Spiritual Arts, and Lotus Light
stops.date_confidence: The 1931 founding of the Society of Spiritual Arts is carried by the dossier from the NYPL papers and from Kimerer LaMothe's scholarship; the month is not established, and no incorporation city was reached, so the coordinates are a New York placeholder. Lotus Light, a book of poems, is dated 1932 in standard library catalogue records.
stops.campa: She founds the Society of Spiritual Arts and turns to the religion she was actually raised in. The goddesses go. What replaces them is the rhythmic choir: groups of women moving in Christian churches to psalms and hymns, dance offered as liturgy instead of as spectacle, in sanctuaries rather than in theatres. The following year she publishes a book of poems, Lotus Light. Critics who had followed her since Radha do not know what to make of any of it and largely stop writing about her.
stops.quote: I feel that I am a link between the invisible world of vision and the visible world of art form.
stops.quote_source: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (Harrap, 1939), ch. XIII 'India Waits at the End of the Journey', p. 277
suggested_refs: Ruth St. Denis, Lotus Light (poems, 1932)

stops.name: Adelphi College, Garden City: dance enters the curriculum
stops.date_confidence: Attested verbatim by Wikipedia's Adelphi University article: 'In 1938, the Dance Program was founded by Ruth St. Denis.' The month is not given. Coordinates corrected to the Garden City campus at 40.720 / -73.652, replacing a figure in the pool that fell 1.7 kilometres east in Westbury.
stops.campa: At Adelphi College on Long Island she founds a dance program, among the first at any American college, at a time when dance in the United States is taught in studios and summer schools and almost nowhere that issues a degree. She takes concert dance out of the theatre, where it has to sell tickets, and puts it in a curriculum, where it only has to be taught. She is fifty-nine. The departments that follow this one will be staffed largely by dancers who left Denishawn, teaching techniques built against hers.
suggested_refs: The Adelphi University Dance Program, founded 1938

stops.name: New York: An Unfinished Life
stops.date_confidence: Harper and Brothers, 1939, per standard catalogue records and the dossier bibliography; the month is not established. The digitised copy consulted for quotations is the Harrap printing at archive.org, dli.ministry.22233. Several page and chapter citations carried in the research pool were wrong and are corrected on the stops that use them.
stops.campa: Harper and Brothers publish her autobiography. She calls it An Unfinished Life, which is accurate in two directions at once: she has thirty years still to run, and the book is less a record than a final performance, the persona sitting down to write its own scripture. She tells the cigarette-poster story again. She writes about Isadora Duncan with real and unforced generosity. She leaves out most of what a biographer would want to know. A Dance Horizons reprint will keep the book in print for another thirty years.
stops.quote: I have always chosen harmonious, mystic, or heroic ideas to dominate my art life. This life has been my religion inasmuch as I have gladly and joyfully shared, worked, sacrificed, endured, and occasionally known a moment of triumph in the interests of this mighty ritual of Beauty.
stops.quote_source: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (Harrap, 1939), ch. XIII 'India Waits at the End of the Journey', p. 277
suggested_refs: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (Harper and Brothers, 1939; Dance Horizons reprint, 1969)

stops.name: New York: the School of Natya, with La Meri
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction resolved against the pool. Wikipedia's La Meri article places the School of Natya in New York City in 1940, La Meri having settled there because of the war, and records that she absorbed it into her Ethnologic Dance Center in 1945. The pool's geography lens had placed the school in Los Angeles with downtown Los Angeles coordinates; that is wrong and is not followed. No street address was located, so the pin is a Manhattan placeholder. The month is unknown.
stops.campa: With La Meri, who is Russell Meriwether Hughes out of Louisville and who has actually studied in several of the countries whose dances she performs, she founds the School of Natya in New York. La Meri has been driven back to America by the war in Europe. She is the trained one, the ethnographer of the pair, and she can name her teachers. St. Denis is sixty-one and is the name over the door. The school teaches what the period calls Oriental dance. Five years on, La Meri folds it into her own Ethnologic Dance Center and the arrangement ends.
suggested_refs: La Meri (Russell Meriwether Hughes), Ethnologic Dance Center, New York

stops.name: Jacob's Pillow, Becket: The Delirium of the Senses, filmed at sixty-two
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction on the date. The 1941 filming of The Delirium of the Senses from Radha rests on the dossier's citation of the Jacob's Pillow film archive; the Wikipedia article on the festival, which was reachable, does not corroborate it, and the month is unknown. Coordinates corrected to 42.2644 / -73.1181, the George Carter Road site given by Wikipedia, replacing a figure in the pool that sat some four kilometres northeast in open country.
stops.campa: At Shawn's farm in the Berkshires, by now a festival and a theatre, she is filmed dancing The Delirium of the Senses from Radha. She is sixty-two. The film is not a record of 1906: it is an old woman restaging a young woman's work in front of a camera, with the intervening thirty-five years visible in every phrase of it. It is close to all that survives in motion of the dance that made her, and everything else is photographs and programmes. She dances it on Shawn's ground, in Shawn's theatre.
suggested_refs: Jacob's Pillow film archive, Ruth St. Denis in The Delirium of the Senses (1941)

stops.name: Jacob's Pillow: Liebestraum at seventy
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The 1949 Liebestraum filming rests on the dossier's citation of the Jacob's Pillow archive and was not independently corroborated; the month is unknown.
stops.campa: She comes back to the Pillow and is filmed again, in Liebestraum, to Liszt. She is seventy, and the piece is not an Asian one: it is a European romantic score danced by an American woman in a long dress, which is what she had been doing before the cigarette poster. The Berkshires belong to Shawn now, his theatre and his festival and his company of men, the whole apparatus he assembled after Denishawn ended and she went west. She comes as a guest, dances the Liszt, and goes back to California.

stops.name: University of Illinois, Urbana: Search for Spiritual Expression
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction on the source rather than the date: the exact date comes from the dossier's citation of a surviving University of Illinois audio recording, which was not itself played this pass. The campus coordinates are confirmed from Wikipedia.
stops.campa: At the University of Illinois she gives a lecture called Search for Spiritual Expression. She is seventy-two, and lecturing is now most of the work: churches, colleges, women's clubs, a circuit of rooms in which a famous dancer explains what dance is for. The rhythmic choirs are twenty years old by now and still going in the churches. The recording survives. On it she is not reminiscing. She is still putting the case she has been putting since Buffalo, that the body is an instrument of religion.

stops.name: 3433 Cahuenga Boulevard West: the studio near Universal City
stops.date_confidence: The address is attested verbatim by Wikipedia; the years she taught there are given only as many, and 1955 orders the segment. Coordinates corrected to 34.1321 / -118.3532, the OSM geocode of the address, replacing a figure in the pool that sat 2.4 kilometres southeast near Franklin Avenue, which contradicted the source's own description of the site as near Universal City. The quotation is her imagined address to young dancers, given inside quotation marks in the memoir, not flat narration.
stops.campa: Her studio stands on Cahuenga Boulevard West near Universal City, on a stretch of road running between the Hollywood Hills and the film lots. She teaches there into her seventies and past them. The students are not going to be Graham or Humphrey; they are young dancers, church groups, people who have heard of her. What she mostly gives them is instruction to disregard what they have been given. Around them in the room are the incense, the brass, the temple furniture, the old costumes folded in trunks.
stops.quote: Remember that the dance is as old as time. Dare to dance your own dance. Do not be bound by the techniques that you have learned, or the criticisms you fear to endure.
stops.quote_source: Ruth St. Denis, An Unfinished Life (Harrap, 1939), ch. XIV 'Denishawn House', p. 330, her imagined address to young dancers

stops.name: Ted Shawn Theatre, Jacob's Pillow: Siddhas of the Upper Air
stops.date_confidence: Date corrected by roughly twenty-three years. The research pool dated this reunion 1941, but Wikipedia's Ted Shawn article ties Siddhas of the Upper Air to their fiftieth anniversary and calls it his final appearance on the stage of the Ted Shawn Theatre; the partnership and the marriage both date from 1914, which puts the fiftieth at 1964, and Shawn, who died in 1972, cannot have made a final stage appearance in 1941. The month within 1964 is not established.
stops.campa: Fifty years after the first joint concert, the two of them walk out together in the Ted Shawn Theatre, in Siddhas of the Upper Air. She is eighty-five and he is seventy-two. They have been married the whole of that time and have lived apart for most of it, on opposite coasts, running separate institutions, never divorced. The siddhas of the title are the perfected ones, who move through the upper air. It is the last time he appears on the stage of his own theatre.
suggested_refs: Siddhas of the Upper Air, Ted Shawn Theatre, Jacob's Pillow

stops.name: Hollywood, Los Angeles: death at eighty-nine
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the date, the cause and the city are confirmed by Wikipedia and corroborated in the dossier from the NYPL record of cause of death. Sources give the place variously as Los Angeles and as Hollywood, which is the same jurisdiction; the pin is Hollywood.
stops.campa: She dies of a stroke in Hollywood, eighty-nine years old, sixty-two years after Radha and four years after the last dance with Shawn in the Berkshires. She had been working to the end: lecturing, teaching in the Cahuenga studio, planning pieces she would not make. The New York Times runs the obituary the following day, and the notices treat her as a founder, which by then is the settled American verdict on her. Shawn outlives her by three and a half years. They were never divorced.
suggested_refs: New York Times obituary, 22 July 1968

stops.name: Forest Lawn, Hollywood Hills: the grave that cannot be confirmed
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and a gap stated as a gap. The interment date is not established by any source reached; the date here repeats the date of death only to order the segment. Wikipedia's raw wikitext carries a category tag placing her burial at Forest Lawn Memorial Park, Hollywood Hills, but the cemetery's own article does not list her among its notable interments, and no plot, marker or primary record was reached. What exists is a category assignment and secondary cemetery-listing pages.
stops.campa: She is buried, by the common account, at Forest Lawn in the Hollywood Hills, a few miles from the Cahuenga studio, in the ground of an industry that never quite worked out what she was. The cemetery does not list her among its notable names. No plot, no marker, no primary record has surfaced in anything reachable. Her dances go on being reconstructed from film, photographs and programmes by people who never saw her work. Where she lies, and under what stone, is not on record.
suggested_refs: Forest Lawn Memorial Park, 6300 Forest Lawn Drive, Hollywood Hills, Los Angeles
